name: Breath
notes: A breath pacer, not a simulation and not a measurement. The instrument's job is to be a metronome for the lungs: audio paces respiration, respiration is a behaviour rather than a cortical rhythm, and respiration has its own well-evidenced route to autonomic and cortical state. Nothing here senses the person, scores them, or verifies that anything happened to them -- the practitioner's own interoception is the only instrument pointed at the body, which is why there are no permissions to grant and no numbers to optimise. The cue is an offer, not a command: everything moves on raised-cosine curves with no transients anywhere, so drifting off the pace produces no sense of having failed.

balanced.label: Balanced — resolved + stable
balanced.note: Resolved like sparse (every adjacent pair 1.22-1.53 ERB apart, so no roughness) but with COPRIME low partials, so the implied fundamental is 36 Hz at every point in the breath rather than drifting an octave. Also has the widest brightness sweep of the three at 11.6 semitones. Seven partials, 216-1188 Hz.

sparse.label: Sparse — resolved, pitch drifts
sparse.note: Resolved (1.07-1.53 ERB) and therefore smooth, but its four lowest partials are all EVEN multiples of 36 -- 6, 8, 10, 12 -- and the first odd partial is 32 dB down. At the bottom of the breath the ear is given harmonics 3, 4 and 5 of 72 Hz, which is squarely the dominance region for virtual pitch, so the implied fundamental is an octave high there and falls to 36 Hz as the breath opens. Pitch dropping while brightness rises is two cues in opposition. Kept as a reference; superseded by balanced.

dense.label: Dense — contiguous
dense.note: Every integer harmonic from 6 to 30, spaced a constant 36 Hz. All 24 adjacent pairs sit inside one critical band (0.26-0.72 ERB), which fuses hard but is also rough. The original set, kept as an A/B reference.

voiceNotes.sets: Two partial sets ship so the choice between them can be made by ear rather than by argument, switchable live mid-breath. Both keep the same 36 Hz lattice and the same unsounded fundamental -- the GCD of each set is 1, so the missing-fundamental percept is intact either way. What differs is critical-band spacing, and therefore roughness. Add more sets here and they appear in the page automatically.
voiceNotes.trim: Per-set level match, and the reason the comparison is worth anything. Measured over a full breath cycle, sparse came out 3.98 dB louder than dense -- easily enough that the louder one wins an A/B on loudness alone regardless of timbre. Dense cannot be trimmed up (it already peaks at 0.795 against the L1 bound and would clip at 1.26), so sparse is trimmed down by that 3.98 dB to meet it. Both now sit at -18.96 dBFS over a cycle. Re-measure and update these if you change any set's partials, cutoffs, or ampFloor.
voiceNotes.crossfadeMs: Time constant for the one-pole smoothing on partial gains. Its real job is making a live set-swap click-free -- gains for partials leaving the set glide to zero rather than dropping -- and at 25 ms it is far shorter than any breath motion, so it is invisible during normal use. Fast enough that an A/B still feels immediate, which matters because auditory memory for timbre is short.
voiceNotes.normalisation: Partial gains are divided by their L1 sum, so |output| <= out * amp arithmetically for any phase relationship. These are exact harmonics of one fundamental and their peaks coincide periodically however the phases are initialised, so an L2 (constant-RMS) normalisation understates the true worst case and clips -- measured at 1.07 before this was fixed. L1 costs headroom but needs no limiter, and a limiter would put frequencies in the air that nobody chose.
voiceNotes.ampFloor: Set well below 1 because L1 normalisation makes the bright end quieter in RMS terms -- energy spreads across more partials -- which would otherwise invert the loudness cue against the brightness cue. That effect was severe with the old 25-partial contiguous set (RMS actually FELL 4 dB from empty to full before this was compensated) and is milder with nine, so the same 0.40 now yields a ~3.5 dB swell toward full rather than ~2. Left as is: monotonic, gentle, and still nothing like a transient.
voiceNotes.out: Lowered from 0.80 to 0.65 when the breath layer was added, and the reason is worth recording: the L1 bound guarantees the DRONE alone stays under out, but noise is not bounded that way, so the total is no longer provable and has to be measured. The binding case is the dense set (crest factor about 7, peaking at 0.795 on its own) plus noise at circular breathing, which measured 0.972 at the old level -- effectively clipping. At 0.65 that worst combination measures about 0.79 with real margin, and everything else sits far below. Claim 12 in verify-breath.js renders every drone-set x layer combination and fails if any of them approaches full scale, which is the replacement for the arithmetic guarantee this layer cost us.

noiseNotes.why: Breath sound IS filtered noise -- turbulent airflow through the airway, shaped by throat and mouth. So this layer is not an analogy for breathing, it is a model of the same physics. That makes the cue iconic rather than arbitrary: the drone has to be learned (brighter means fuller), while this means what it resembles.
noiseNotes.amplitudeTracksFlow: The crucial detail. `openness` is lung VOLUME, but breath sound is produced by AIRFLOW, which is its derivative. The raised-cosine openness curve differentiates analytically -- flow is proportional to sin(pi*p)/duration -- so the envelope costs no new parameters and comes out physically right: it swells and fades within each inhale and exhale, loudest in the middle, and is exactly zero through any retention. Holding your breath makes no sound, and the model produces that for free rather than needing a rule for it.
noiseNotes.flowRef: Flow that maps to full noise level, in openness-units per second. 1.31 is the peak flow of the fastest shipped cycle (circular at 25/min), so that protocol reaches the top of the range and slower ones sit below it.
noiseNotes.flowGamma: Compression exponent on flow. 1.0 would be physically literal -- 14 dB between a slow resonance exhale and circular breathing. 0.8 keeps faster protocols audibly more effortful (about 8 dB) while leaving slow breathing clearly audible rather than nearly silent. Raise toward 1.0 for more contrast between protocols, lower for less.
noiseNotes.tilts: Real breath differs by direction: inhale is brighter and more turbulent, exhale lower and broader. The sign of the flow derivative tells us which without any extra state, so the two directions get different filter centres and stop being acoustic mirror images. This is a cue dimension the drone does not have.
noiseNotes.layering: The drone stays underneath as the anchor. Noise alone would go silent through retentions -- correct physically, but box breathing is 50 percent holds, so half the cycle would have no cue at all and the timing reference would vanish. Layers are independently switchable so that can be heard rather than argued about.

safetyNotes.maxExhaleHoldSeconds: Hard cap, applied at load time to every phase of every protocol regardless of what the protocol asks for. Empty-lung retention after heavy ventilation is the shallow-water-blackout mechanism, and a retention is the one segment where the practitioner is deliberately overriding the urge to breathe -- so it is the one place 'listen to your body' is weakest and a fixed number has to do the work instead. Not user-adjustable by design.
safetyNotes.maxSessionMinutes: Total wall-clock cap on a session.
safetyNotes.abortGlideSeconds: How long the instrument takes to glide from wherever it is into the abort phase's cycle. Abort must never cut to silence -- an abrupt stop in a deep state is its own problem -- so it decelerates into slow breathing instead.

cycleNotes.shape: Every phase names a breath cycle as four durations in seconds: inhale, inhaleHold, exhale, exhaleHold. Absolute seconds rather than rate-plus-ratio because that is how protocols are actually written (4-7-8, box 4-4-4-4). Rate is derived from the sum, not configured.
cycleNotes.zero: Zero is a legal value for any of the four. Circular and connected breathing is defined by having no pauses at all, so {1.2, 0, 1.2, 0} has to produce a seamless turnaround rather than a special case. The raised-cosine openness curve has zero derivative at both ends of inhale and exhale, so the apex is smooth without needing a crossfade.
cycleNotes.direction: Heart rate rises during inhale (vagal withdrawal) and falls during exhale (vagal return), so exhale-dominant cycles are calming and inhale-dominant cycles are activating. Both are legitimate; the engine does not prefer either. This note is documentation for whoever writes a protocol, not a constraint the code enforces.
cycleNotes.ramps: A phase interpolates from one cycle to another. Interpolating four-tuples means a ramp can change rate and shape at once -- {4,0,6,0} to {1.5,0,1.5,0} both accelerates and migrates from exhale-dominant to symmetric, which is what a real settle-to-ramp transition does. from equal to to gives a steady phase, so there is no separate case.

resonance.label: Resonance — slow paced breathing
resonance.about: Slow exhale-weighted breathing at 6/min. Sits at the baroreflex resonance near 0.1 Hz, where respiratory and blood-pressure oscillations phase-align and heart rate oscillations amplify. 5.5/min is the population mode and the fixed rate that outperformed nothing and matched individualised resonance frequency in a four-week trial -- so this is a default to start from and adjust by feel, not a target to hit.

box.label: Box — 4-4-4-4
box.about: Equal quarters with both retentions. Included because it is the protocol that exercises all four segments at once, which is what the cue has to stay legible through.

ramp-test.label: Ramp test — 6/min to 25/min and back
ramp-test.about: Not a practice protocol. It exists to stress the two ends the cue has to work at simultaneously: a 10-second cycle where every segment is long and slow, and a 2.4-second circular cycle with no holds at all, where the inhale/exhale turnaround happens twice a second. If the cue reads clearly at both without clicking at the apex, the engine is right.

protocolNotes.phases: Ordered. Each runs for `seconds`, or until the practitioner advances it when `untilUserInput` is true. A user-terminated retention is both more faithful to how retentions are actually practised -- held until you need to breathe, not for a number someone else chose -- and safer, because it returns the decision to the person.
protocolNotes.abortTo: Names the phase that the abort control glides into. Defaults to the last phase if absent.
